title: The month of Jeth
hookLine: in Jeth, join with the One before whom all bow (Barah Maha, ang 134)

lines: MAY INTO JUNE: THE ROADS SHIMMER.
cards: By late morning the roads shimmer. Shops pull their shutters halfway down. This is Jeth, roughly May into June in Punjab, hot in a way that changes how people live.
Anyone who can stays indoors through the afternoon, and the dust storms called aandhi can turn the sky brown. In that heat, even the proudest person slows down and looks for shade.
Nobody walks tall at two in the afternoon in Jeth. And this is the month Guru Arjan chooses to talk about the One before whom every head goes down.

teach.b: The Jeth stanza is on ang 134. It opens, in paraphrase: in Jeth, the longing is to be joined with the Lord, before whom everyone bows. Not some.
Everyone. Kings and laborers, the clever and the simple, the powerful and the poor are all, sooner or later, lowered. The heat makes that easy to picture.

Then an image of safety: one who holds the hem of the beloved Friend's robe can't be bound by anyone. It's an old picture, a child or a petitioner clinging to the edge of someone's garment, and protected.
Then a picture of riches. The Name of the One is like rubies and pearls, and no thief can break in to steal them. In an old village, valuables could be stolen and houses broken into.
Here is wealth no one can carry off. The stanza goes on: the One does whatever pleases the One, and creatures act accordingly; those the One makes His own are called blessed.
And it ends: in Jeth, the joyful Lord is met by the one whose forehead carries that good fortune.

teach.h: HOLDING THE HEM OF THE FRIEND.
teach.b: Put the pieces together: bowing, holding on, a treasure that can't be stolen.
Jeth's lesson isn't about pushing through the heat on your own strength.
It's about lowering yourself and holding on.
In a month when everything outside presses down, the stanza turns the pressure into a bow.

how: On the sangrand of Jeth, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Jeth stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the summer heat, especially around the remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls serving cold sweetened water to passersby.

o: the month of hard heat, when every head bows
the midday rest when shops close their shutters
a dust storm that turns the sky brown

games.q: the month of Jeth — tap the pairs.
p: May into June, the month of heat
hold it and none can bind you

s: the Jeth stanza says only the humble bow to the One
it says everyone bows before the One.
the stanza compares the Name to rubies and pearls
a treasure no thief can break in to steal.
the stanza's picture of safety is holding the Friend's hem
one who holds it can't be bound by anyone.

games.q: it's a burning afternoon in Jeth and everything presses down on you. what does the stanza's picture suggest?
o: push through on your own strength.
bow, and hold on to the hem of the Friend.
games.why: in Jeth the longing is to join the One before whom all bow; one who holds the Friend's hem can't be bound.

practice: Notice one pressure on you right now, tiredness, a deadline, real heat, a weight in the chest, and don't push against it.

Breathe in, and as you breathe out, lower your head slowly, as if bowing to something greater than the pressure; stay low a breath or two, picturing the edge of a friend's robe in your hand, then rise.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.

wordCard.voice: Jeth. The month of hard heat, when Guru Arjan longs to be joined with the One before whom everyone bows, whose Name is a treasure no thief can steal.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: in Jeth, a month of fierce heat in the Punjabi year; the stanza's opening.

carryVoice: Your line: jeth: bow. Some treasures are out of every thief's reach. That's five hundred sixty-eight.
